strings.qada_d_coma_p1: The nearest rule Nur al-Idah gives is for the gravely ill: someone unable even to signal the prayer with a nod of the head has up to five such prayers postponed and made up, and is excused any beyond five.
strings.qada_d_coma_p1_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Prayer Of A Sick Person
strings.qada_d_coma_p2: Not made up. Loss of consciousness is treated like loss of reason. The one exception is a prayer whose time had already partly run before consciousness was lost: that prayer is owed.
strings.qada_d_coma_p2_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f1.1, f2.6
strings.qada_d_coma_p3: The Risala does not take up a prolonged loss of consciousness in its chapter on making up missed prayers.
strings.qada_d_coma_p4: The base text has him make up every prayer missed during the coma, treating it like sleep rather than like insanity. The translator’s note records that the other three schools — and a present-day fatwa council — hold the opposite, that nothing is made up unless he woke before the prayer’s time ended.
strings.qada_d_coma_p4_src: Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 10: The Prayer of The Sick — Making up for the Missed Prayers
strings.qada_d_coma_subject: Prayers missed while unconscious or in a prolonged coma.
strings.qada_d_excused_p1: Sleep and forgetfulness are the excuses named in the hadith the school relies on. Leaving a prayer knowingly, out of laziness, is a sin the state disciplines — and the prayer is still owed until it is prayed and repented for.
strings.qada_d_excused_p1_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Ruling With Respect To The Order Of Prayer; Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Ruling Of One Who Neglects Prayer
strings.qada_d_excused_p2: Three, and only three: you were asleep when the time came and stayed asleep until it ended; you forgot; or you put the prayer back to combine it with another on a journey. Nothing else excuses letting the time pass.
strings.qada_d_excused_p3: A prayer forgotten or slept through is made up with no disagreement. A prayer left out on purpose is also made up, on the school’s settled position. What the excuse changes is the sin and the delay allowed, not whether it is owed.
strings.qada_d_excused_p4: Umdat al-Fiqh is an abridgement and does not set out the excuses. The one case it treats is the person unconscious in a coma — see the next card.
strings.qada_d_excused_subject: Which reasons for missing a prayer count as excused.
strings.qada_d_many_p1: Once six prayers are owed, the requirement to keep them in order falls away for good. They are simply made up, in any order.
strings.qada_d_many_p1_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — That Which Excuses The Order
strings.qada_d_many_p2: Keeping the order was only ever recommended, so a backlog carries no ordering burden. The duty to hurry — for prayers missed without an excuse — is measured against all your free time.
strings.qada_d_many_p2_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f2.7, f2.8
strings.qada_d_many_p3: A large backlog may be made up at any hour, including sunrise and sunset when prayer is otherwise held back. The relief is for the hardship; the prayers are still worked through steadily, not shelved.
strings.qada_d_many_p4: Umdat al-Fiqh states that a missed obligatory prayer may be made up at any time, including the prohibited hours. It does not treat a large backlog as a case of its own.
strings.qada_d_many_p4_src: Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 8: Times When Salat Is Prohibited
strings.qada_d_many_subject: What eases a large backlog of missed prayers.
strings.qada_d_order_lift_p1: Any of three things: too little of the preferred prayer-time is left for both the missed and the current prayer; you forgot the missed prayer; or the missed prayers reach six. Once lifted it does not return, even if you later bring the number back below six.
strings.qada_d_order_lift_p1_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — That Which Excuses The Order
strings.qada_d_order_lift_p2: Nothing needs to lift it, because keeping the order was only ever recommended.
strings.qada_d_order_lift_p3: Owing five or more prayers, together with the fear of losing the current prayer’s time — then the current prayer is prayed first.
strings.qada_d_order_lift_p4: Umdat al-Fiqh states no order rule, so it states no exception.
strings.qada_d_order_lift_subject: What lifts the requirement to keep the order.
strings.qada_d_order_p1: Necessary (wajib). The missed prayer comes before the current one, and missed prayers are kept in their own order too — as long as they are fewer than six.
strings.qada_d_order_p1_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Ruling With Respect To The Order Of Prayer
strings.qada_d_order_p2: Only recommended. Making up missed prayers before the current one, and in the order they were missed, is preferred but not required; and if the current prayer’s time would otherwise run out, it is prayed first.
strings.qada_d_order_p2_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f2.8, f2.9
strings.qada_d_order_p3: Obligatory while the missed prayers are few — fewer than a full day and night, meaning fewer than five. They are prayed before the current one even if its time then passes, and a current prayer already prayed is prayed again afterwards.
strings.qada_d_order_p4: Umdat al-Fiqh does not say whether a make-up is prayed before or after the current prayer.
strings.qada_d_order_subject: Whether a missed prayer must be prayed before the current one.
strings.qada_d_soon_p1: Nur al-Idah sets no general deadline. What it fixes is the order: while your missed prayers are few, each is prayed before the next current prayer (the section below). Someone who left a prayer knowingly is in sin until it is prayed.
strings.qada_d_soon_p1_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Ruling With Respect To The Order Of Prayer; Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Ruling Of One Who Neglects Prayer
strings.qada_d_soon_p2: Missed with an excuse: making it up at once is recommended. Missed without one: making it up at once is obligatory — in every hour not taken by life’s necessities — and that person may not pray voluntary prayers at all until the make-ups are finished.
strings.qada_d_soon_p3: Making up a missed prayer at once is obligatory, and delay is not allowed except for an excuse. Where the missed prayers are many, they are worked through steadily rather than all at once — but not left to drift.
strings.qada_d_soon_p4: Umdat al-Fiqh gives no general rule on how soon. It states only that a make-up may be prayed at any time, including the hours when voluntary prayer is otherwise held back.
strings.qada_d_soon_p4_src: Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 8: Times When Salat Is Prohibited
strings.qada_d_soon_subject: How quickly a missed prayer must be made up.
strings.qada_editions: Each school’s position is cited to a manual of that school: Reliance of the Traveller for Shafi’i, Nur al-Idah for Hanafi, The Risala for Maliki, Umdat al-Fiqh for Hanbali. Section numbers follow the English editions listed here.
strings.qada_hadith_edition: Hadith numbering follows the numbering used on Sunnah.com, which generally aligns with widely published editions.
strings.qada_intro: A prayer whose time ends before you have prayed it is a missed prayer, and it is made up. Making it up is called qada. Missing prayers is the single most common thing a new Muslim has to deal with, and it is not a mark against you: the make-up is the way back that the law itself provides. This guide covers what must be made up, how soon, in what order, and where the four schools differ.
strings.qada_s1_before_islam: A new Muslim does not make up the prayers of the years before Islam. Nothing was owed then, so nothing is owed now. In the Shafi’i manual the same is true of prayers missed while insane, or during an illness that takes away awareness — those are not made up either.
strings.qada_s1_before_islam_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f1.1; Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — Conditions That Obligate Prayer
strings.qada_s1_body: A prayer is “missed” once its time ends without your having prayed it. It does not stop being owed — it becomes a debt you make up when you are able. Making up a missed prayer is qada; praying it inside its time is ada.
strings.qada_s1_cause: The reason a prayer was missed matters. Missing it because you were asleep, genuinely forgot, or were unconscious is treated as excused. Missing it while awake, aware and able is not. It is made up either way — but the excuse changes how urgent the make-up is, and whether the missing was itself a sin. The schools draw that line in their own places, marked through this guide.
strings.qada_s1_cause_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f1.5; Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Ruling Of One Who Neglects Prayer; The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 12.4a
strings.qada_s1_hadith: The Prophet ﷺ said, “Whoever misses a prayer through sleep or forgetfulness should pray it as soon as he remembers; there is no other amends for it.”
strings.qada_s1_hadith_src: Sahih al-Bukhari 597; Sahih Muslim 684. Also quoted in The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 12.4a
strings.qada_s1_heading: What counts as a missed prayer
strings.qada_s2_body: All four schools hold that a missed obligatory prayer must be made up, whatever the reason it was missed. Scholars have reported agreement on this.
strings.qada_s2_body_src: Reliance of the Traveller, w18.6, w18.8
strings.qada_s2_deliberate: This holds even for a prayer left out on purpose. The four schools agree it is still made up: the sin is in the neglect, and the make-up is what puts it right. The Maliki and Hanafi manuals say so directly; for the Shafi’i and Hanbali schools it is reported in Reliance’s survey, which cites their manuals al-Majmu‘ and al-Mughni.
strings.qada_s2_deliberate_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f2.7, w18.6, w18.8; The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 12.4a, 12.4c; Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Ruling Of One Who Neglects Prayer
strings.qada_s2_minority: A few scholars outside the four schools — Ibn Hazm, and later Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn al-Qayyim — held that a prayer left out deliberately until its time is gone can never be made up, only repented for and outweighed with good deeds. All four schools reject this, and it is not the position this guide follows.
strings.qada_s2_minority_src: Reliance of the Traveller, w18.6, w18.9
strings.qada_s2_note: If you have missed prayers — one, or years of them — the answer is not despair. Make them up as you are able. That is not a punishment added on; it is the way back that the law itself holds open.
strings.qada_s3_body: Every school wants the make-up done without needless delay. How binding that is — and how much an excuse loosens it — is where they part.
strings.qada_s3_heading: How soon a missed prayer is made up
strings.qada_s4_body: Asr’s time has come and you still have not prayed Dhuhr — which comes first? This is the point on which Nur al-Idah has a whole chapter and the schools diverge most.
strings.qada_s4_heading: Missed and current prayers, and the order between them
strings.qada_s5_body: The new Muslim who embraced Islam late, or the person returning to prayer after years away, faces not one missed prayer but hundreds. The schools make this lighter, not heavier.
strings.qada_s5_heading: When there are many missed prayers
strings.qada_s5_tail: None of this reaches back before Islam: a convert makes up only what was missed since becoming Muslim.
strings.qada_s5_tail_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f1.1; Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — Conditions That Obligate Prayer
strings.qada_s6_body: A woman does not pray during her monthly period, or during postnatal (afterbirth) bleeding — and, unlike every other missed prayer, these are not made up afterwards. All four schools agree. For those days the obligation to pray is simply lifted, so there is no debt to repay; over a lifetime the prayers would otherwise be an impossible number.
strings.qada_s6_body_src: Reliance of the Traveller, e13.4; Nur al-Idah, Book i: Purification — The Chapter Of Menstrual Periods, Postnatal and Chronic Vaginal Discharge; The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 2.2f; Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 1 ch. 9: Hayd (The Menstrual Period)
strings.qada_s6_edges: Two edges are worth knowing. If bleeding begins after enough of a prayer’s time has passed for you to have prayed it, that prayer was already due and is owed. And a woman looks for the end of her bleeding as each prayer time comes in — becoming pure with time left to wash and pray means that prayer counts. Only the prayers wholly within the bleeding are dropped.
strings.qada_s6_edges_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f2.6; The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 2.2f
strings.qada_s6_fasts: The fasts are the contrast. A day of Ramadan missed because of bleeding is made up later; the prayers of those days are not. This is asked constantly, and easy to get the wrong way round.
strings.qada_s6_fasts_src: Reliance of the Traveller, e13.4; Nur al-Idah, Book i: Purification — The Chapter Of Menstrual Periods, Postnatal and Chronic Vaginal Discharge
strings.qada_s6_hadith: A’isha was asked why a woman makes up the fasts she misses in her period but not the prayers. She answered, “That would happen to us, and we were ordered to make up the fast and were not ordered to make up the prayer.”
strings.qada_s6_heading: Prayers missed during menstruation and postnatal bleeding
strings.qada_s7_body: The clearest answer is the Shafi’i one: a person who missed a prayer without a valid excuse may not pray voluntary prayers until every make-up is done. A prayer missed with an excuse does not carry that bar.
strings.qada_s7_heading: Voluntary prayers while make-ups are outstanding
strings.qada_s7_others: Nur al-Idah, The Risala and Umdat al-Fiqh do not rule on the question in the parts read for this guide. All three, though, require a missed prayer to be made up without needless delay, which points the same way. Nur al-Idah adds that even a voluntary prayer, once begun and then broken, must itself be made up.
strings.qada_s7_others_src: The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 12.4a; Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Prohibited And Disliked Prayer Times
strings.qada_s8_adhan: The call to prayer is given for a make-up. For a single missed prayer, the adhan and the iqama both; for a run of them, the adhan once at the start and the iqama for each. Nur al-Idah and Reliance are close to agreed on this; The Risala has the iqama for every one.
strings.qada_s8_adhan_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f3.5; Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — Calling The Adhan And Iqama For Missed Prayers; The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 12.4a
strings.qada_s8_body: A make-up is the same prayer, prayed the same way. You are paying the debt in the coin it was owed.
strings.qada_s8_count: It has the raka’at the prayer has: Fajr two, Maghrib three, the rest four. In the Hanafi and Maliki schools the make-up follows your state when the time ran out — a prayer missed while resident is made up in full even if you are travelling now, and one missed while travelling is made up shortened even if you are resident now.
strings.qada_s8_count_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — Making Up Missed Prayers; The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 12.4a
strings.qada_s8_group: A make-up may be prayed in congregation by people who missed the same prayer: the Prophet ﷺ led the Companions in four prayers they had all missed at the Battle of the Trench, with the adhan and iqama called for each. Where a group is praying the current prayer and you still owe an earlier one, Reliance has you make up the earlier prayer on your own first.
strings.qada_s8_group_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — Calling The Adhan And Iqama For Missed Prayers; Reliance of the Traveller, f2.10
strings.qada_s8_heading: How a make-up prayer is performed
strings.qada_s8_recitation: It is recited aloud or silently as the prayer itself is — Fajr, Maghrib and Isha aloud, Dhuhr and Asr silently. The Shafi’i school ties this instead to the time you make it up in: aloud if you would normally recite aloud then, silently otherwise. The Risala also has you say the qunut when making up Subh.
strings.qada_s8_recitation_src: The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 12.4a; Reliance of the Traveller, f8.25
strings.qada_s8_unsure: If you know you missed one of the five but not which, the Shafi’i school has you pray all five, each with the intention of the make-up.
strings.qada_s9_agree_1: A missed obligatory prayer is made up, whatever the reason — including one left out on purpose.
strings.qada_s9_agree_2: A prayer is made up with the number of raka’at it was owed with.
strings.qada_s9_agree_3: Prayers missed during menstruation or postnatal bleeding are not made up; the fasts of those days are.
strings.qada_s9_agree_4: A new Muslim does not make up the prayers of the years before Islam.
strings.qada_s9_agree_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f1.1, f2.7, e13.4; Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Ruling With Respect To The Order Of Prayer; Nur al-Idah, Book i: Purification — The Chapter Of Menstrual Periods, Postnatal and Chronic Vaginal Discharge; The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 12.4a; Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 1 ch. 9: Hayd (The Menstrual Period)
strings.qada_s9_body: Under the differences above, all four schools hold that:
strings.qada_s9_differ: They differ on the points this guide marks: how soon the make-up must be done, whether the order between missed and current prayers binds and when it lifts, what eases a large backlog, whether voluntary prayers may be prayed while make-ups are owed, and how a make-up’s recitation is decided.
strings.qada_src_nur: Nur al-Idah, Hasan al-Shurunbulali — Hanafi. Book ii (Prayer), including the chapters on making up missed prayers and the order of prayer, and Book i (Purification) on menstruation, were read directly for this guide.
strings.qada_src_reliance: Reliance of the Traveller (Umdat al-Salik), Ahmad ibn Naqib al-Misri, tr. Nuh Ha Mim Keller — Shafi’i. Book f (f1–f3, f8), Book e (e13) and the appendix w18 were read directly for this guide.
strings.qada_src_risala: The Risala, Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani, tr. Bello Mohammad Daura, with the commentary of al-Azhari — Maliki. Chapter 12 (missing a prayer), chapter 2 (menstruation) and chapter 23 (fasting) were read directly for this guide.
strings.qada_src_umdah: Umdat al-Fiqh, Ibn Qudamah al-Maqdisi, translated with commentary by Hatem al-Haj — Hanbali. Book 2 (the prayer of the sick; the prohibited times) and Book 1 (menstruation) were read directly. This edition is an abridgement: where it does not cover a question, the guide says so.
strings.qada_summary: Making up a prayer whose time has passed
strings.qada_unreviewed: No qualified scholar has checked this guide. Every ruling in it was checked against a manual of the school it is credited to, and names where — but that verifies the transcription, not the fiqh. Treat this as a draft and ask someone qualified before you rely on it.
